A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BPR ranking and decision-aware training work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–E are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic experiments, the Appendix B ranking demonstration, and forecasting results for Massachusetts overdoses, Cook County overdoses, and endangered cranes.

after.justification: V3 retains original synthetic and forecasting results and adds empirical comparisons with other training methods and forecasting baselines.

M1.justification: The ratio estimator, score-function gradients, perturbed top-K optimization, DAML objective, model families, and Algorithm A.1 are retained. The alternative estimator discussed in new Appendix B.1 is not adopted into the procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same seven-site synthetic experiment, nine-site ranking demonstration, Massachusetts and Cook County overdose datasets, and ANWR crane dataset. Added comparisons use existing forecasting tasks and populations.

E2.justification: Figure 3 adds evaluated PG and SPO+ comparators across all three real-world tasks. New Table C.2 also compares last-timestep, historical-average, chance/zero-prediction, and EpiGNN baselines on cranes and Cook County, substantially broadening comparison beyond the original training objectives.

E3.justification: Table C.2 adds MAE and RMSE evaluation. New comparator protocols specify shared models and ranking estimators, validation-based tuning, and special initializations for PG/SPO+ on cranes. Existing task splits, K values, and DAML hyperparameter ranges remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The synthetic misspecification study and Appendix B ranking demonstration are retained. No new ablation, sensitivity, distribution-shift, or robustness study is reported; Table C.2 extends model/metric benchmarking rather than adding a separate diagnostic experiment.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 1,000 ranking trials with 1,000 samples per ranking, 10,000 toy trials, and 20 synthetic initializations. V3 clarifies that Figure 3 uncertainty concerns BPR while likelihood is a point estimate, without changing the statistical reporting procedure.

E6.justification: V3 adds PG/SPO+ results and Table C.2's MAE/RMSE/BPR entries; for example, crane EpiGNN obtains RMSE 0.70 and BPR 0.06. Figure 3 also revises retained crane results: its new caption places DAML above BPR-only, although Section 5.3 still states the reverse.

T1.justification: Section 2 adds an explicit time-invariant conditional data-distribution assumption. Appendix B.1 introduces the top-K-denominator estimator and asserts equivalence to the existing ratio estimator without a supporting proof. Existing bound derivations and gradient formulas are retained.

C1.justification: The conclusion extends the claimed advantage in likelihood–BPR tradeoffs from conventional training to previous decision-aware methods. The abstract's central ranking and constrained-training contributions remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: V3 discusses applicability under temporal distribution change and limits conclusions to the studied misspecification types. It also suggests sparsity as an explanation for comparator optimization difficulties and explains why favorable MAE/RMSE can coexist with poor BPR.

D1.justification: V3 identifies PyEPO as the PG/SPO+ implementation and documents additional baseline construction and tuning information. Massachusetts data are now described as publicly available upon request rather than private. Existing code access, DAML hyperparameters, and model implementation appendices are retained.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning within operations research and decision-focused learning, including surveys, resource-allocation applications, Directed Regression, PG, and SPO+. It explicitly distinguishes DAML's constrained nonconvex objective and connects the task to knapsack optimization.

P1.justification: V3 locally rewrites the introduction, training explanations, and application descriptions; adds related-work and appendix subheadings; and moves the conditional model setup into Section 2. The overall section sequence and most methodological exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn with additional comparator markers, expanded legends, changed axes, and a revised caption, and is separated from Figure 2 onto another page. Table C.2 adds two side-by-side result panels; Figures 1–2 and existing appendix tables remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses v1's narrow empirical comparison through relevant decision-focused baselines and Table C.2, which makes forecasting-error versus decision-quality tradeoffs more assessable. Expanded positioning and applicability caveats also help. These gains are limited by the unsupported estimator-equivalence assertion in Appendix B.1 and the conflicting crane rankings in Figure 3's caption and Section 5.3.
